newsitem.title: UK: Controversy mounts over shooting of IRA suspect.
newsitem.headline: Controversy mounts over shooting of IRA suspect.

text.p: British police were on Saturday given more time to question four IRA suspects but controversy mounted over the shooting dead of an unarmed man during raids in London which netted 10 tonnes of explosives.
The parents of the dead man Diarmuid O"Neill, described their son as "kind, unselfish and loving" and accused police of taking the law into their own hands.

A later search of the room in which he was living revealed no weapons. His younger brother Shane, who was also among those arrested in the police swoop on Monday, was freed on Friday pending further inquiries.
Police applied for more time under Britain's anti-terrorist laws to question the four remaining suspects but must charge or release them by Monday.
Irish-born Eoghan and Theresa O"Neill said on Friday they were relieved that Shane had been released.

"Our eldest son, Diarmuid, was never arrested; he can never be tried, nor can he be acquitted or convicted other than by the press...Instead, those who accused him took the law into their own hands and killed him," they said in a statement.
"Diarmuid was a kind, unselfish and loving son whom we loved dearly all his life," they added.
The haul of explosives and weapons was initially hailed as a crushing blow to Irish Republican Army morale.
It also ended speculation that the guerrillas were preparing to call a new ceasefire in their campaign against British rule of Northern Ireland.

But British authorities have been put on the defensive by reports that O"Neill was unarmed when he was shot, prompting memories of the 1988 murders of three unarmed suspected guerrillas by commandos in the British colony of Gibraltar.
Amnesty International has accused police of making misleading statements over the death of O'Neill and called for an independent judicial inquiry into the shooting.
Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA"s political wing Sinn Fein, on said on Friday that O"Neill was killed in "very disputable circumstances".
Speaking on a British radio phone-in programme, Adams said; "As far as I can tell he was a decent law-abiding, good, honest young man."
